issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: Michael, a 49-year-old European-American married man and City Council Member, has been struggling with intrusive memories and maladaptive coping strategies since his combat experience. The traumatic event was a pivotal moment in which he faced intense enemy fire during a mission that left several of his comrades dead or wounded. Michael's account of the incident is fragmented; he can only recall flashes of chaos and terror, but not the full sequence of events. Since returning home, Michael has found himself constantly on edge, unable to trust that even familiar environments are truly safe. The memory gaps about the event have left him with a sense that there’s more to remember—fragments that could still be lurking in his mind. This incomplete picture makes it difficult for him to fully process what happened and cope with the aftermath. Michael has developed several maladaptive strategies as a result of these fragmented memories. He often turns to loud music or television, which he finds helps distract from the persistent thoughts about combat and the fear that comes with them. Additionally, he is constantly monitoring his own thoughts for any signs of going crazy, convinced that his mind might unravel at any moment. These distractions help manage some of the anxiety but also serve as a reminder that the trauma continues to intrude on his daily life. His marriage has been strained by these changes. Any form of physical contact with his wife now triggers an intense startle response, and he avoids being touched altogether. Even when others assure him that he is safe at home or work, Michael finds it impossible to believe them. His world view has shifted dramatically—now, he perceives the world as a dangerous place where vigilance is necessary for survival. When Michael tries to explain what happened during combat to his wife or colleagues, he often loses track of his thoughts and cannot finish his sentences. The terror that accompanies these memories makes it particularly difficult for him to articulate them clearly. He has come to believe that his body is betraying him—reacting as if he were still in danger even when he knows rationally that he is safe. The memory gaps, combined with the fear of remembering more, have created a cycle of hypervigilance and anxiety. Michael feels like he must always be on guard, scanning for threats both real and imagined. This constant state of alertness makes it difficult for him to relax or sleep properly, leading to significant sleep problems. Michael’s maladaptive strategies serve as temporary relief but also reinforce the negative appraisals about his safety and the world around him. By constantly monitoring his thoughts and seeking sensory distractions, he avoids facing the incomplete memories directly, which keeps them active and painful. His belief that the world is a dangerous place has become more entrenched over time, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of fear and avoidance. These patterns have started to take a toll on Michael’s work as a City Council Member. He finds it hard to concentrate during meetings, often distracted by intrusive thoughts or physical reactions to sudden movements or sounds. His colleagues have noticed the changes in his behavior but are unsure how to support him effectively. What finally brought Michael to seek help was a realization that he could no longer function at work and maintain any semblance of peace at home. He is most afraid of losing control, both emotionally and physically, and hopes for some relief from the constant terror that haunts him. His primary goal is to find ways to manage his reactions so that he can regain a sense of normalcy in his life and relationships. Despite the overwhelming nature of these symptoms, Michael remains hopeful that therapy will help him understand and manage his traumatic memories more effectively. He wants to reclaim control over his body and mind without feeling like he’s always living on edge.
